h1:
Phae Mueang Phi
Strange Earth Pillars in the Phrae Forest
intro: Phae Mueang Phi is one of those spots that makes people look at a photo and ask, "Is this really Thailand?" Wind and rain have eaten away at the soil and rock for ages, leaving behind tall pillars and oddly shaped cliffs you can walk around in a loop. It sits just about 12–15 kilometres from Phrae town, so it's an easy stop and more fun to photograph than you'd expect.

blocks.html: Phae Mueang Phi is a small forest park shaped entirely by nature. The ground here is loosely packed sand and gravel, and after a very long time of rain washing it down and wind scouring it, the softer soil has slowly disappeared, leaving only the firmer columns standing as pillars and odd-looking earthen walls. Some have a rock capping the top like a hat. People call this kind of terrain "earth pillars" — geologically, hoodoos, similar to what you find in Cappadocia in Turkey, just on a smaller scale.

The name "Phae Mueang Phi" comes from the local dialect — "phae" means scrubland, while "mueang phi" (city of ghosts) comes from the quiet atmosphere and the sound of wind passing through the pillars, plus a folk tale about an old woman who found treasure in the forest and couldn't find her way out. It became a name that sounds mysterious enough to stick to this day.

A few hundred metres in from the car park, you reach the first cluster of earth pillars — a basin shaped like an upturned pan, roughly 30 metres wide and a hundred-odd metres long, ringed with earthen columns in strange shapes. Some are slim and tall like posts, others stout like mushrooms or termite mounds. The soil leans brownish-orange, which contrasts nicely with the green trees around it.

items: Main pillar field — the most striking group and the easiest to photograph, near the entrance and a short walk in
Eroded earth cliffs — tall, layered earthen walls grooved by the rain, where you can clearly see the bands in the soil
Nature study trail — a loop of about 3 kilometres through deciduous dipterocarp forest, with distant views all the way to Doi Phra That Cho Hae on a clear day
Elevated viewpoint — some sections look down on the rows of earth pillars, good for wide-angle shots

blocks.title: Which walk to pick
blocks.html: If you're short on time or have older relatives along, just doing the main pillar-field loop covers all the highlights and takes under an hour. If you like hiking, add the 3-kilometre nature study trail. The path is dirt and gets slippery in spots after rain, so shoes you're comfortable walking in will serve you better.

Phae Mueang Phi is an easy forest park to visit, and the fee is very cheap — around 20 THB for adults and 10 THB for children (seniors usually get in free). At times it works on a donation box at the entrance instead. It's good value for what you get to see. It's open daily, roughly 08:30–16:30 (some sources say until 17:00). It's worth checking the forest park's page again before you go, in case hours shift with the season.

items: Entry fee — about ฿20 for adults · about ฿10 for children (sometimes a donation box)
Time needed — short loop ~45 min · full nature study trail ~1.5–2 hours
Facilities — car park, restrooms, and a few small food stalls by the parking area

blocks.html: The pillars photograph best under low-angled sun — early morning around 08:00–10:00 or late afternoon from 15:30 until closing, when the slanted light gives the pillar surfaces texture and nice shadows. Around midday the sun is directly overhead, so it gets hot and the shots come out flatter. As for seasons, the cool months (November–February) have the nicest weather and the most comfortable walking. In the rainy season the soil colours look richer, but the paths are slippery, so take a little care.

blocks.title: A little prep
blocks.html: There isn't much shade here, so bring water, a hat, and sunscreen, especially if you go during the day. School holidays and weekends draw bigger crowds than weekdays — if you want clear, empty shots, an early weekday morning is your best bet.

Phae Mueang Phi sits in the Nam Cham–Thung Hong area of Mueang Phrae district, about 12–15 kilometres from town. Driving from the city takes just 15–20 minutes: head out along Highway 101 (the Phrae–Nan route) for about 9–12 kilometres, then turn off at the junction and follow the signs for another 6 kilometres or so. The access road is fairly good and an ordinary car handles it easily.

items.name: Driving / your own rental car
items.blurb: The most convenient option, with a wide car park in front of the forest park. Good for pairing with other nearby sights on the same trip.

items.name: Motorbike
items.blurb: Rent one in Phrae town and ride out yourself. The route isn't complicated, so it suits solo travellers or couples.

items.name: Chartered songthaew / taxi
items.blurb: No public bus runs to the entrance, so you'll need to charter a round trip. Expect around ฿700–800 depending on how you negotiate.

blocks.html: The handy thing about Phae Mueang Phi is that it sits right on the way out of town toward Phra That Cho Hae, so you can combine the two in half a day. Stop in the morning to pay respects at Phra That Cho Hae, the temple that's a symbol of Phrae, then come on to stroll Phae Mueang Phi in the late morning before heading back into town for lunch. If you still have energy, carry on to the old town and the teak-house cafés in the afternoon.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee for Phae Mueang Phi?
faq.a: The fee is very cheap — about 20 THB for adults and 10 THB for children, and seniors usually get in free. At times it works on a donation box at the entrance instead. It's good value for the views you get.

faq.q: What are Phae Mueang Phi's opening hours?
faq.a: It's open daily, roughly 08:30–16:30 (some sources say until 17:00). The best light for photos is in the morning around 08:00–10:00 or in the late afternoon from 15:30 onward.

faq.q: How far is Phae Mueang Phi from Phrae town?
faq.a: It's about 12–15 kilometres away, just a 15–20 minute drive from the city. Take Highway 101 on the Phrae–Nan route, then turn off at the junction and follow the signs for another 6 kilometres or so.

faq.q: Can I visit Phae Mueang Phi without a private vehicle?
faq.a: No public bus runs to the entrance. The easiest option is to rent a car or motorbike in town and drive yourself. Without a vehicle, you'll need to charter a songthaew or taxi for the round trip, which costs around 700–800 THB.

faq.q: Is it a long walk, and how long does it take?
faq.a: If you just do the main pillar-field loop, it takes under an hour to see all the highlights. If you enjoy hiking, you can add the nature study trail for another 3 kilometres or so, which takes about 1–1.5 hours more.
